claim: Presenilin-1 (PS1)/γ-secretase is required for axon growth in the developing mouse brain.
source: We show that presenilin-1 (PS1)/γ-secretase is required for axon growth in the developing mouse brain.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced axon length in Psen1-/- mouse brains and cultured neurons (Figure 1).

claim: PS1/γ-secretase mediates axon growth by inhibiting RhoA signaling.
source: PS1/γ-secretase mediates axon growth by inhibiting RhoA signaling and cleaving EphA3 independently of ligand to generate an intracellular domain (ICD) fragment that reverses axon defects in PS1/γ-secretase- and EphA3-deficient hippocampal neurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that RhoA inhibition reverses axon defects in PS-deficient neurons (Figure 5).

claim: PS1/γ-secretase cleaves EphA3 independently of ligand to generate an intracellular domain (ICD) fragment.
source: PS1/γ-secretase mediates axon growth by inhibiting RhoA signaling and cleaving EphA3 independently of ligand to generate an intracellular domain (ICD) fragment that reverses axon defects in PS1/γ-secretase- and EphA3-deficient hippocampal neurons.
evidence: Supported by biochemical analyses showing EphA3 ICD generation and its ability to reverse axon defects (Figures 2, 3).

claim: EphA3 ICD reverses axon defects in PS1/γ-secretase- and EphA3-deficient hippocampal neurons.
source: PS1/γ-secretase mediates axon growth by inhibiting RhoA signaling and cleaving EphA3 independently of ligand to generate an intracellular domain (ICD) fragment that reverses axon defects in PS1/γ-secretase- and EphA3-deficient hippocampal neurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that EphA3 ICD expression rescues axon length in deficient neurons (Figure 3).

claim: EphA3 ICD binds to non-muscle myosin IIA (NMIIA).
source: Proteomic analysis revealed that EphA3 ICD binds to non-muscle myosin IIA (NMIIA) and increases its phosphorylation (Ser1943), which promotes NMIIA filament disassembly and cytoskeleton rearrangement.
evidence: Supported by proteomic analysis and co-immunoprecipitation assays (Figure 6A, B).

claim: EphA3 ICD increases NMIIA phosphorylation at Ser1943.
source: Proteomic analysis revealed that EphA3 ICD binds to non-muscle myosin IIA (NMIIA) and increases its phosphorylation (Ser1943), which promotes NMIIA filament disassembly and cytoskeleton rearrangement.
evidence: Supported by biochemical data showing increased phosphorylated NMIIA in EphA3 ICD-expressing neurons (Figure 6C).

claim: NMIIA phosphorylation at Ser1943 promotes NMIIA filament disassembly and cytoskeleton rearrangement.
source: Proteomic analysis revealed that EphA3 ICD binds to non-muscle myosin IIA (NMIIA) and increases its phosphorylation (Ser1943), which promotes NMIIA filament disassembly and cytoskeleton rearrangement.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about NMIIA phosphorylation and experimental data showing changes in NMIIA localization (Figure 6D).

claim: PS1/γ-secretase-deficient neurons show decreased phosphorylated NMIIA.
source: PS1/γ-secretase-deficient neurons show decreased phosphorylated NMIIA and NMIIA/actin colocalization.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and biochemical data (Figure 6C, D).

claim: PS1/γ-secretase-deficient neurons show decreased NMIIA/actin colocalization.
source: PS1/γ-secretase-deficient neurons show decreased phosphorylated NMIIA and NMIIA/actin colocalization.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claim: Pharmacological NMII inhibition reverses axon retraction in PS-deficient neurons.
source: Moreover, pharmacological NMII inhibition reverses axon retraction in PS-deficient neurons suggesting that NMIIA mediates PS/EphA3-dependent axon elongation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing blebbistatin treatment rescues axon defects (Figure 6E).

claim: NMIIA mediates PS/EphA3-dependent axon elongation.
source: Moreover, pharmacological NMII inhibition reverses axon retraction in PS-deficient neurons suggesting that NMIIA mediates PS/EphA3-dependent axon elongation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that NMII inhibition reverses axon defects in PS-deficient neurons.

claim: PS/γ-secretase-dependent EphA3 cleavage mediates axon growth by regulating filament assembly through RhoA signaling and NMIIA.
source: In conclusion, PS/γ-secretase-dependent EphA3 cleavage mediates axon growth by regulating filament assembly through RhoA signaling and NMIIA, suggesting opposite roles of EphA3 on inhibiting (ligand-dependent) and promoting (receptor processing) axon growth in developing neurons.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental data showing the involvement of RhoA and NMIIA in PS/EphA3-mediated axon growth (Figures 5, 6).

claim: EphA3 has opposite roles on inhibiting (ligand-dependent) and promoting (receptor processing) axon growth in developing neurons.
source: In conclusion, PS/γ-secretase-dependent EphA3 cleavage mediates axon growth by regulating filament assembly through RhoA signaling and NMIIA, suggesting opposite roles of EphA3 on inhibiting (ligand-dependent) and promoting (receptor processing) axon growth in developing neurons.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that ephrin-A5 binding inhibits axon growth while EphA3 ICD promotes it (Figures 3, 4).

claim: Axon length is significantly reduced (~50%) in 4 days in vitro (DIV) cultured hippocampal neurons from Psen1-/- embryos.
source: In agreement with the in vivo results, axon length was significantly reduced (~50%) in 4 days in vitro (DIV) cultured hippocampal neurons from Psen1-/- embryos, but not Psen2-/- embryos, or treated with the γ-secretase inhibitors DAPT or the broad-spectrum ADAM/matrix metalloproteinase inhibitor GM6001 (p<0.05; Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of axon length in cultured neurons shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Axon length is not significantly reduced in 4 DIV cultured hippocampal neurons from Psen2-/- embryos.
source: In agreement with the in vivo results, axon length was significantly reduced (~50%) in 4 days in vitro (DIV) cultured hippocampal neurons from Psen1-/- embryos, but not Psen2-/- embryos, or treated with the γ-secretase inhibitors DAPT or the broad-spectrum ADAM/matrix metalloproteinase inhibitor GM6001 (p<0.05; Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Treatment with the γ-secretase inhibitor DAPT reduces axon length in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: In agreement with the in vivo results, axon length was significantly reduced (~50%) in 4 days in vitro (DIV) cultured hippocampal neurons from Psen1-/- embryos, but not Psen2-/- embryos, or treated with the γ-secretase inhibitors DAPT or the broad-spectrum ADAM/matrix metalloproteinase inhibitor GM6001 (p<0.05; Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Treatment with the broad-spectrum ADAM/matrix metalloproteinase inhibitor GM6001 reduces axon length in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: In agreement with the in vivo results, axon length was significantly reduced (~50%) in 4 days in vitro (DIV) cultured hippocampal neurons from Psen1-/- embryos, but not Psen2-/- embryos, or treated with the γ-secretase inhibitors DAPT or the broad-spectrum ADAM/matrix metalloproteinase inhibitor GM6001 (p<0.05; Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: PS/γ-secretase and metalloprotease activities are required for axon growth in hippocampal neurons.
source: These results strongly indicate that PS/γ-secretase and metalloprotease activities are required for axon growth in hippocampal neurons.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that inhibition of either PS/γ-secretase or metalloproteases reduces axon length (Figure 1D).

claim: Neurofilament staining is largely absent in processes and restricted to the cytoplasm of doublecortin-positive immature neurons in Psen1-/- hippocampus.
source: Notably, neurofilament staining is largely absent in processes and restricted to the cytoplasm of doublecortin-positive immature neurons in Psen1-/- hippocampus (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The number of doublecortin-positive immature neurons is unchanged in Psen1-/- brains.
source: The axon length defects are unlikely due to global changes on the abundance of doublecortin-positive immature neurons since number of these cells are unchanged in Psen1-/- brains (Handler et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Handler et al., 2000.

claim: Reduced staining of neurofilament- and tau-stained axons and nestin filaments is observed in the outer layer of the hippocampus and ventricular zone of Psen1-/- embryos.
source: Immunolabeling and confocal microscope analysis revealed reduced staining of neurofilament- and tau-stained axons and nestin filaments in the outer layer of the hippocampus and ventricular zone of Psen1-/- embryos (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A, B.

claim: Axon length defects in Psen1-/- brains are confirmed by retrograde DiI labeling.
source: Axon length defects in Psen1-/- brains were confirmed by retrograde DiI labeling (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by DiI labeling data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Psen1-/- mouse embryos show enlarged ventricles and brain hemorrhages.
source: PS1 is essential for brain development as revealed by abundant brain hemorrhages, enlarged ventricles and neuron migration defects in Psen1-/- mouse embryos (Shen et al., 1997; Hartmann et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shen et al., 1997 and Hartmann et al., 1999.

claim: Psen1-/- mouse embryos show neuron migration defects.
source: PS1 is essential for brain development as revealed by abundant brain hemorrhages, enlarged ventricles and neuron migration defects in Psen1-/- mouse embryos (Shen et al., 1997; Hartmann et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shen et al., 1997 and Hartmann et al., 1999.

claim: Epha3, 4, 7 and 8 mRNAs decrease significantly coinciding with last stages of axon elongation (4–7 DIV).
source: Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) revealed differential expression of multiple EphA transcripts in cultured hippocampal neurons. Interestingly, Epha3, 4, 7 and 8 mRNAs decrease significantly coinciding with last stages of axon elongation (4–7 DIV; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: EphA3 is highly expressed in axons where it regulates axon growth of hippocampal neurons in the developing brain.
source: We focused specifically on EphA3 since: (1) EphA3 is highly expressed in axons where it regulates axon growth of hippocampal neurons in the developing brain (Yue et al., 2002; Kudo et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citations to Yue et al., 2002 and Kudo et al., 2005.

claim: EphA3 protein is elevated at initial stages of axon polarization and elongation (2–4 DIV) and then it significantly decreases.
source: (2) EphA3 protein is elevated at initial stages of axon polarization and elongation (2–4 DIV) and then it significantly decreases (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by biochemical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Binding of ephrin-A5 to EphA3 induces the interaction of the metalloproteinase ADAM10 causing the cleavage in trans of ephrin-A5.
source: (3) binding of ephrin-A5 to EphA3 induces the interaction of the metalloproteinase ADAM10 causing the cleavage in trans of ephrin-A5 (Janes et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Janes et al., 2005.

claim: EphA3 is expressed as a punctuate pattern at the actin-enriched growth cones and filopodia, and along axons in hippocampal neurons.
source: Notably, EphA3 is expressed as a punctuate pattern at the actin-enriched growth cones and filopodia, and along axons in hippocampal neurons, where it highly colocalizes with PS1 (~50%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: EphA3 highly colocalizes with PS1 (~50%) in hippocampal neurons.
source: Notably, EphA3 is expressed as a punctuate pattern at the actin-enriched growth cones and filopodia, and along axons in hippocampal neurons, where it highly colocalizes with PS1 (~50%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: PS1 binds to EphA3 in brain extracts of postnatal mouse brains.
source: Notably, coimmunoprecipitation assays revealed binding of PS1 to EphA3 in brain extracts of postnatal mouse brains, as well as in HEK293 cells overexpressing both proteins but not PS1 alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: PS1 binds to EphA3 in HEK293 cells overexpressing both proteins but not PS1 alone.
source: Notably, coimmunoprecipitation assays revealed binding of PS1 to EphA3 in brain extracts of postnatal mouse brains, as well as in HEK293 cells overexpressing both proteins but not PS1 alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: An endogenous EphA3 C-terminal derived fragment (CTF, ~49 kDa) accumulates in PS1-/- embryonic mouse brains.
source: Biochemical analysis using polyclonal (C-19) and monoclonal (5E11F2) anti-C-terminal EphA3 antibodies revealed accumulation of an endogenous EphA3 C-terminal derived fragment (CTF,~49 kDa) in PS1-/- embryonic mouse brains and cultured neurons (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A, B.

claim: An endogenous EphA3 C-terminal derived fragment (CTF, ~49 kDa) accumulates in PS1-/- cultured neurons.
source: Biochemical analysis using polyclonal (C-19) and monoclonal (5E11F2) anti-C-terminal EphA3 antibodies revealed accumulation of an endogenous EphA3 C-terminal derived fragment (CTF,~49 kDa) in PS1-/- embryonic mouse brains and cultured neurons (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A, B.

claim: The EphA3 CTF (~49 kDa) is a PS/γ-secretase substrate.
source: This suggests that this fragment could be a PS/γ-secretase substrate.
evidence: Inferred from the accumulation of EphA3 CTF in PS1-/- cells and upon γ-secretase inhibition.

claim: DAPT increases EphA3 CTFs in EphA3-HA expressing HEK293 cells.
source: DAPT increases EphA3 CTFs in EphA3-HA expressing HEK293 cells, as detected with an anti-HA antibody (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: EphA3 CTFs are present in lysates of EphA3-transfected Psen1-/-/Psen2-/- mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEF) but not in control (Psen1+/+/Psen2+/+) or non-transfected Psen1-/-/Psen2-/- MEFs.
source: EphA3 CTFs were also present in lysates of EphA3-transfected Psen1-/-/Psen2-/-mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEF) but not in control (Psen1+/+/Psen2+/+) or non-transfected Psen1-/-/Psen2-/- MEFs (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The ADAM/matrix metalloproteinase inhibitors MMP9/13, GM6001 and 1,10-phenanthroline (1,10-PNT) reduce accumulation of EphA3 CTFs in HEK293 cells treated with γ-secretase inhibitors.
source: These compounds reduced significantly accumulation of EphA3 CTFs in HEK293 cells treated with the γ-secretase inhibitors DAPT or L-685,458 indicating EphA3 shedding by metalloprotease/ADAM (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2E, F.

claim: EphA3 shedding is mediated by metalloprotease/ADAM.
source: These compounds reduced significantly accumulation of EphA3 CTFs in HEK293 cells treated with the γ-secretase inhibitors DAPT or L-685,458 indicating EphA3 shedding by metalloprotease/ADAM (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that metalloprotease inhibitors reduce EphA3 CTF accumulation.

claim: An EphA3 N-terminal derived fragment (NTF, ~75 kDa) is significantly reduced in conditioned media in the presence of the MMP9/13 inhibitor.
source: Furthermore, an EphA3 N-terminal derived fragment (NTF,~75 kDa) was significantly reduced in conditioned media in the presence of the MMP9/13 inhibitor (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: EphA3 ICD (~47–49 kDa) is generated in a time- and DAPT-dependent manner in the soluble (S100) fraction of transfected HEK293 cells.
source: Biochemical analysis revealed generation of EphA3 ICD (~47–49 kDa) in a time- and DAPT-dependent manner in the soluble (S100) fraction of transfected HEK293 cells, and the presence of endogenous EphA3 ICD in mouse brain lysates (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by in vitro γ-secretase assay data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Endogenous EphA3 ICD is present in mouse brain lysates.
source: Biochemical analysis revealed generation of EphA3 ICD (~47–49 kDa) in a time- and DAPT-dependent manner in the soluble (S100) fraction of transfected HEK293 cells, and the presence of endogenous EphA3 ICD in mouse brain lysates (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by in vitro γ-secretase assay data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The PS/γ-secretase cleavage site in EphA3 is at amino acid Y560.
source: Proteomic analysis of trypsin-digested gel samples (~47–49 kDa band) revealed the presence of a major VLIGR peptide, corresponding to EphA3 (aa 561–565) indicating that the γ-secretase cleavage occurs at aminoacid Y560 (Figure 2H; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS proteomic analysis shown in Figure 2H and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Sequential cleavage of EphA3 by metalloprotease/ADAM and PS1/γ-secretase occurs in neurons.
source: These results demonstrate sequential cleavage of EphA3 by metalloprotease/ADAM and PS1/γ-secretase in neurons (Figure 2I).
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental data showing metalloprotease-dependent shedding and PS/γ-secretase-dependent ICD generation (Figure 2).

claim: EphA3 ICD, but not EphA3 full-length or ΔICD, reverses axon length defects in Psen1-/- and/or DAPT-treated hippocampal neurons.
source: Confocal imaging analysis shows that EphA3 ICD, but not EphA3 full-length or ΔICD, reversed axon length defects in Psen1-/- and/or DAPT-treated hippocampal neurons (Figure 3A,B), suggesting that PS1/γ-secretase-dependent EphA3 ICD generation is sufficient for axon growth.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A, B.

claim: PS1/γ-secretase-dependent EphA3 ICD generation is sufficient for axon growth.
source: Confocal imaging analysis shows that EphA3 ICD, but not EphA3 full-length or ΔICD, reversed axon length defects in Psen1-/- and/or DAPT-treated hippocampal neurons (Figure 3A,B), suggesting that PS1/γ-secretase-dependent EphA3 ICD generation is sufficient for axon growth.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that EphA3 ICD alone can rescue axon defects.

claim: EphA3 ICD recovers axon length in vehicle- or DAPT-treated EphA3-deficient neurons.
source: Moreover, EphA3 ICD recovered axon length in vehicle- or DAPT-treated EphA3-deficient neurons and reduced significantly the percentage of collapsed growth cones in Psen1-/- neurons (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: EphA3 ICD reduces significantly the percentage of collapsed growth cones in Psen1-/- neurons.
source: Moreover, EphA3 ICD recovered axon length in vehicle- or DAPT-treated EphA3-deficient neurons and reduced significantly the percentage of collapsed growth cones in Psen1-/- neurons (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In utero electroporation assays show a significant decrease of axon length in the ventricular zone of Psen1-/- embryos (E16.5).
source: In utero electroporation assays showed a significant decrease of axon length in the ventricular zone of Psen1-/- embryos (E16.5; p<0.0001; Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by in utero electroporation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: No significant differences in axon length are found in EphA3 ICD expressing Psen1+/+ and Psen1-/- brains.
source: Notably, no significant differences in axon length in EphA3 ICD expressing Psen1+/+ and Psen1-/- brains were found (p=0.61).
evidence: Supported by in utero electroporation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: PS/γ-secretase regulates axon elongation through EphA3 processing.
source: Together, these results indicate that PS/γ-secretase regulates axon elongation through EphA3 processing.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental data showing that EphA3 ICD rescues axon defects in PS-deficient neurons (Figure 3).

claim: Ephrin-A5 efficiently enhances EphA3 phosphorylation (Tyr779) and binding to the downstream effector CrkII.
source: As previously shown (Lawrenson et al., 2002), ephrin-A5 efficiently enhanced EphA3 phosphorylation (Tyr779) and binding to the downstream effector CrkII (Figures 2B and 4A).
evidence: Supported by biochemical data shown in Figures 2B and 4A, and citation to Lawrenson et al., 2002.

claim: DAPT does not significantly affect EphA3 phosphorylation.
source: Notably, DAPT did not affect significantly EphA3 phosphorylation, whereas ephrin-A5 increased EphA3 signaling without major changes on EphA3 CTFs in hippocampal neurons or HEK293 (Figures 2D and 4A).
evidence: Supported by biochemical data shown in Figures 2D and 4A.

claim: Ephrin-A5 increases EphA3 signaling without major changes on EphA3 CTFs in hippocampal neurons or HEK293.
source: Notably, DAPT did not affect significantly EphA3 phosphorylation, whereas ephrin-A5 increased EphA3 signaling without major changes on EphA3 CTFs in hippocampal neurons or HEK293 (Figures 2D and 4A).
evidence: Supported by biochemical data shown in Figures 2D and 4A.

claim: Ephrin-A5 reduces axon length by triggering EphA3 signaling in hippocampal neurons.
source: In agreement with previous reports (Nishikimi et al., 2011), ephrin-A5 reduced axon length by triggering EphA3 signaling in hippocampal neurons (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B and citation to Nishikimi et al., 2011.

claim: Ephrin-A5 does not cause additional effects in Epha3 shRNA- or DAPT-treated neurons.
source: Ephrin-A5 did not cause additional effects in Epha3 shRNA- or DAPT-treated neurons suggesting that ephrin-A5 regulates negatively axon growth through EphA3 signaling (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Ephrin-A5 regulates negatively axon growth through EphA3 signaling.
source: Ephrin-A5 did not cause additional effects in Epha3 shRNA- or DAPT-treated neurons suggesting that ephrin-A5 regulates negatively axon growth through EphA3 signaling (Figure 4B).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ephrin-A5 has no additional effect in EphA3-deficient neurons.

claim: Epha3 knockdown mimics and occludes the effect of PS/γ-secretase inhibition on axon elongation in the presence or absence of ephrin-A5.
source: Epha3 knockdown mimicked and occluded the effect of PS/γ-secretase inhibition on axon elongation in the presence or absence of ephrin-A5 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Human EphA3 full-length, but not mutants lacking the ligand-binding (ΔLBD) or PDZ (ΔPDZ) domains, recovers axon length defects in Epha3-deficient hippocampal neurons.
source: Human EphA3 full-length, but not mutants lacking the ligand-binding (ΔLBD) or PDZ (ΔPDZ) domains, recovered axon length defects in Epha3-deficient hippocampal neurons (Figure 4C,D; and data not shown).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C, D.

claim: PS1/γ-secretase mediates axon growth through ligand-independent EphA3 signaling.
source: These results strongly suggest that PS1/γ-secretase mediates axon growth through ligand-independent EphA3 signaling.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that ephrin-A5 does not affect EphA3 processing and that EphA3 ICD can rescue axon defects independently of ligand (Figure 4).

claim: The Rho-kinase inhibitor Y27632 induces an overall significant increase on axon growth in Psen1+/+/Psen1-/- and Veh/DAPT-treated hippocampal neurons.
source: The Rho-kinase inhibitor Y27632 induced an overall significant increase on axon growth in Psen1+/+/Psen1-/- (p<0.0002) and Veh/DAPT-treated (p<0.0066) hippocampal neurons (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A, B.

claim: Y27632 and a dominant-negative RhoA mutant (RhoA T19N) efficiently reverse axon length defects in Psen1- and γ-secretase activity-deficient neurons.
source: Importantly, Y27632 and a dominant-negative RhoA mutant (RhoA T19N) efficiently reversed axon length defects in Psen1- and γ-secretase activity-deficient neurons (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: EphA3-ICD is not able to rescue axon defects in DAPT-treated hippocampal neurons in the presence of the constitutive active RhoA mutant (RhoA Q63L).
source: EphA3-ICD was not able to rescue axon defects in DAPT-treated hippocampal neurons in the presence of the constitutive active RhoA mutant (RhoA Q63L), which suggests that EphA3 acts upstream of RhoA (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: EphA3 acts upstream of RhoA.
source: EphA3-ICD was not able to rescue axon defects in DAPT-treated hippocampal neurons in the presence of the constitutive active RhoA mutant (RhoA Q63L), which suggests that EphA3 acts upstream of RhoA (Figure 5D).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that constitutively active RhoA blocks EphA3 ICD rescue effects.

claim: EphA3-ICD expression significantly reduces RhoA activity in SK-N-AS neuronal cells.
source: EphA3-ICD expression significantly reduced RhoA activity in SK-N-AS neuronal cells although it did not apparently affect RhoA activity in primary neurons in these experimental conditions (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: Supported by RhoA activity assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: EphA3-ICD does not apparently affect RhoA activity in primary neurons in these experimental conditions.
source: EphA3-ICD expression significantly reduced RhoA activity in SK-N-AS neuronal cells although it did not apparently affect RhoA activity in primary neurons in these experimental conditions (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: Supported by RhoA activity assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Ephrin-A5 increases RhoA activity in hippocampal neurons.
source: As previously shown in cancer cells (Lawrenson et al., 2002), ephrin-A5 increased RhoA activity in hippocampal neurons, whereas DAPT significantly increased and caused a synergistic effect on RhoA activation (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by RhoA activity assay data shown in Figure 5F and citation to Lawrenson et al., 2002.

claim: DAPT significantly increases RhoA activity and causes a synergistic effect on RhoA activation with ephrin-A5.
source: As previously shown in cancer cells (Lawrenson et al., 2002), ephrin-A5 increased RhoA activity in hippocampal neurons, whereas DAPT significantly increased and caused a synergistic effect on RhoA activation (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by RhoA activity assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: PS/γ-secretase-dependent EphA3 cleavage is unlikely to mediate axon elongation by affecting only RhoA signaling.
source: These results suggest that PS/γ-secretase-dependent EphA3 cleavage is unlikely to mediate axon elongation by affecting only RhoA signaling.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that EphA3 ICD does not consistently affect RhoA activity in primary neurons.

claim: Proteomic analysis identified three specific prominent protein bands of ~85, ~200 and ~250 kDa corresponding to heat shock protein (HSP), clathrin heavy chain one and non-muscle myosin IIA heavy chain (NMIIA), respectively.
source: Interestingly, we identified three specific prominent protein bands of ~85,~200 and~250 kDa corresponding to heat shock protein (HSP), clathrin heavy chain one and non-muscle myosin IIA heavy chain (NMIIA), respectively (Figure 6A; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by proteomic analysis shown in Figure 6A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Casein kinase II-mediated phosphorylation (Ser1943) of NMIIA heavy chain promotes cytoskeleton rearrangement by inhibiting assembly and/or promoting disassembling of myosin/F-actin/microtubule filaments and cell motility.
source: In addition, casein kinase II-mediated phosphorylation (Ser1943) of NMIIA heavy chain promotes cytoskeleton rearrangement by inhibiting assembly and/or promoting disassembling of myosin/F-actin/microtubule filaments and cell motility (Dulyaninova and Bresnick, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dulyaninova and Bresnick, 2013.

claim: EphA3 ICD interacts with NMIIA heavy chain.
source: Biochemical assays revealed that EphA3 ICD interacts with NMIIA heavy chain, and elevates axonal phosphorylated (Ser1943) NMIIA heavy chain especially in Psen1-/- hippocampal neurons (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: EphA3 ICD elevates axonal phosphorylated (Ser1943) NMIIA heavy chain especially in Psen1-/- hippocampal neurons.
source: Biochemical assays revealed that EphA3 ICD interacts with NMIIA heavy chain, and elevates axonal phosphorylated (Ser1943) NMIIA heavy chain especially in Psen1-/- hippocampal neurons (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: γ-secretase-deficient hippocampal neurons show decreased total phosphorylated NMIIA.
source: Indeed, γ-secretase-deficient hippocampal neurons show decreased total phosphorylated NMIIA and phosphorylated NMIIA/actin colocalization in axons (Figure 6D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that γ-secretase inhibition could stabilize membrane cytoskeleton-associated NMIIA resulting in assembly or blocking disassembly of filaments.
evidence: Supported by biochemical data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: γ-secretase-deficient hippocampal neurons show decreased phosphorylated NMIIA/actin colocalization in axons.
source: Indeed, γ-secretase-deficient hippocampal neurons show decreased total phosphorylated NMIIA and phosphorylated NMIIA/actin colocalization in axons (Figure 6D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that γ-secretase inhibition could stabilize membrane cytoskeleton-associated NMIIA resulting in assembly or blocking disassembly of filaments.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: γ-secretase inhibition could stabilize membrane cytoskeleton-associated NMIIA resulting in assembly or blocking disassembly of filaments.
source: Indeed, γ-secretase-deficient hippocampal neurons show decreased total phosphorylated NMIIA and phosphorylated NMIIA/actin colocalization in axons (Figure 6D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that γ-secretase inhibition could stabilize membrane cytoskeleton-associated NMIIA resulting in assembly or blocking disassembly of filaments.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of decreased phosphorylated NMIIA and increased insoluble NMIIA in γ-secretase-deficient neurons.

claim: DAPT-treated hippocampal neurons show a significant decrease of soluble NMIIA.
source: In support of this, biochemical assays show a significant decrease of soluble, increase of insoluble and unchanged total NMIIA levels in DAPT-treated hippocampal neurons (Figure 6D, and not shown).
evidence: Supported by biochemical data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: DAPT-treated hippocampal neurons show an increase of insoluble NMIIA.
source: In support of this, biochemical assays show a significant decrease of soluble, increase of insoluble and unchanged total NMIIA levels in DAPT-treated hippocampal neurons (Figure 6D, and not shown).
evidence: Supported by biochemical data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: DAPT-treated hippocampal neurons show unchanged total NMIIA levels.
source: In support of this, biochemical assays show a significant decrease of soluble, increase of insoluble and unchanged total NMIIA levels in DAPT-treated hippocampal neurons (Figure 6D, and not shown).
evidence: Stated in the text but data not shown.

claim: A non-phosphorylated S1943A NMIIA mutant decreases significantly axon length in hippocampal neurons.
source: Indeed, a non-phosphorylated S1943A NMIIA mutant decreased significantly axon length in hippocampal neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Blebbistatin increases axon length in DAPT-treated hippocampal neurons.
source: Interestingly, blebbistatin, a specific inhibitor that binds to the myosin-ADP-Pi complex maintaining NMII in an actin-detached state (Kovács et al., 2004), increased axon length and occluded the effect of EphA3-ICD in DAPT-treated hippocampal neurons (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6E and citation to Kovács et al., 2004.

claim: Blebbistatin occludes the effect of EphA3-ICD in DAPT-treated hippocampal neurons.
source: Interestingly, blebbistatin, a specific inhibitor that binds to the myosin-ADP-Pi complex maintaining NMII in an actin-detached state (Kovács et al., 2004), increased axon length and occluded the effect of EphA3-ICD in DAPT-treated hippocampal neurons (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: An inactive blebbistatin enantiomer has no significant effects on axon length.
source: By contrast, an inactive blebbistatin enantiomer had not significant effects (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: EphA3 acts upstream of NMIIA to promote disassembly or to prevent assembly of NMIIA/actin filaments in axons.
source: These results strongly suggest that EphA3 acts upstream of NMIIA to promote disassembly or to prevent assembly of NMIIA/actin filaments in axons.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that EphA3 ICD increases NMIIA phosphorylation and that blebbistatin occludes EphA3 ICD effects (Figure 6).

claim: Eph/ephrin signaling regulates axon growth and guidance of neurons.
source: EphA/ephrin signaling regulates axon growth and guidance of neurons, but whether this process occurs also independently of ephrins is unclear.
evidence: Established knowledge in the field.

claim: It is unclear whether Eph/ephrin signaling regulates axon growth independently of ephrins.
source: EphA/ephrin signaling regulates axon growth and guidance of neurons, but whether this process occurs also independently of ephrins is unclear.
evidence: Stated as an open question in the field.

claim: Rho plays a critical role in the regulation of axon initiation, elongation, guidance and collapse by regulating the assembly, disassembly and rearrangement of the actin and microtubule cytoskeleton.
source: Rho plays a critical role in the regulation of axon initiation, elongation, guidance and collapse by regulating the assembly, disassembly and rearrangement of the actin and microtubule cytoskeleton (Hall and Lalli, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hall and Lalli, 2010.

claim: RhoA regulates negatively axon growth by activating ROCK.
source: RhoA regulates negatively axon growth by activating ROCK, whereas the Rho members Rac and Cdc42 promote axon growth in hippocampal neurons (Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2007.

claim: The Rho members Rac and Cdc42 promote axon growth in hippocampal neurons.
source: RhoA regulates negatively axon growth by activating ROCK, whereas the Rho members Rac and Cdc42 promote axon growth in hippocampal neurons (Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2007.

claim: ROCK inhibits axon growth by blocking depolymerization of actin filaments indirectly by activating LIM kinase that phosphorylates ADF/cofilin.
source: ROCK inhibits axon growth by blocking depolymerization of actin filaments indirectly by activating LIM kinase that phosphorylates ADF/cofilin, and directly by increasing phosphorylation and activating myosin II light chain (MLC) resulting in contraction of actin fibers (Da Silva et al., 2003; Govek et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Da Silva et al., 2003 and Govek et al., 2005.

claim: ROCK inhibits axon growth directly by increasing phosphorylation and activating myosin II light chain (MLC) resulting in contraction of actin fibers.
source: ROCK inhibits axon growth by blocking depolymerization of actin filaments indirectly by activating LIM kinase that phosphorylates ADF/cofilin, and directly by increasing phosphorylation and activating myosin II light chain (MLC) resulting in contraction of actin fibers (Da Silva et al., 2003; Govek et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Da Silva et al., 2003 and Govek et al., 2005.

claim: Non-muscle myosin IIA (NMIIA)/myosin-9 promotes neurite retraction caused by repulsive signals in neurons.
source: In neurons, non-muscle myosin IIA (NMIIA)/myosin-9 promotes neurite retraction caused by repulsive signals (Wylie and Chantler, 2003; Kubo et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wylie and Chantler, 2003 and Kubo et al., 2008.

claim: Phosphorylation of NMIIA heavy chain by several kinases, including protein kinase C (PKC) or casein kinase 2 (CKII), prevents formation and/or disassembles myosin filaments.
source: Phosphorylation of NMIIA heavy chain by several kinases, including protein kinase C (PKC) or casein kinase 2 (CKII), prevents formation and/or disassembles myosin filaments (Breckenridge et al., 2009; Dulyaninova and Bresnick, 2013), although the role of NMIIA phosphorylation in axodendritic morphology is unknown.
evidence: Supported by citations to Breckenridge et al., 2009 and Dulyaninova and Bresnick, 2013.

claim: The role of NMIIA phosphorylation in axodendritic morphology is unknown.
source: Phosphorylation of NMIIA heavy chain by several kinases, including protein kinase C (PKC) or casein kinase 2 (CKII), prevents formation and/or disassembles myosin filaments (Breckenridge et al., 2009; Dulyaninova and Bresnick, 2013), although the role of NMIIA phosphorylation in axodendritic morphology is unknown.
evidence: Stated as an unknown aspect in the field.

claim: The Eph family of receptor tyrosine kinases and their cell-attached ephrin ligands inhibit axon growth by mediating growth cone collapse through regulation of Ras and Rho GTPases.
source: The Eph family of receptor tyrosine kinases and their cell-attached ephrin ligands inhibit axon growth by mediating growth cone collapse through regulation of Ras and Rho GTPases (Noren and Pasquale, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Noren and Pasquale, 2004.

claim: Binding of ephrins to EphA or EphB receptors of opposing cells triggers Eph phosphorylation and recruitment of cytoplasmic proteins, such as CrkII, resulting in cell-cell repulsive signals.
source: Binding of ephrins to EphA or EphB receptors of opposing cells triggers Eph phosphorylation and recruitment of cytoplasmic proteins, such as CrkII, resulting in cell-cell repulsive signals.
evidence: Established knowledge in the field.

claim: Binding of ephrinA1 to EphA4 induces Rho GEF ephexin-1 binding, which triggers RhoA activation and consequently induces growth cone collapse in hippocampal neurons.
source: For instance, binding of ephrinA1 to EphA4 induces Rho GEF ephexin-1 binding, which triggers RhoA activation and consequently induces growth cone collapse in hippocampal neurons (Shamah et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shamah et al., 2001.

claim: Binding of ephrin-A5 to EphA induces growth cone collapse in a RhoA/ROCK-dependent manner.
source: Binding of ephrin-A5 to EphA induces growth cone collapse in a RhoA/ROCK-dependent manner (Gao et al., 1999; Wahl et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gao et al., 1999 and Wahl et al., 2000.

claim: EphA3 signaling regulates elongation and navigation of axons and trajectories and assembly of spinal motor neuron axons.
source: EphA3 signaling, a relevant regulator of cell migration and neurite and axon outgrowth (Shi et al., 2010), regulates elongation and navigation of axons and trajectories and assembly of spinal motor neuron axons (Marquardt et al., 2005; Gallarda et al., 2008; Nishikimi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Marquardt et al., 2005, Gallarda et al., 2008, and Nishikimi et al., 2011.

claim: Eph/ephrin-mediated repulsive signals in developing neurons are largely limited to cell-cell contacts during axon guidance.
source: Eph/ephrin-mediated repulsive signals in developing neurons are largely limited to cell-cell contacts during axon guidance.
evidence: Established knowledge in the field.

claim: It is unclear whether Eph receptors regulate axon elongation independently of classical ephrin signaling.
source: At present, it is unclear whether Eph receptors regulate axon elongation independently of classical ephrin signaling, but a mechanism involving shedding of ephrin ligands and receptors was recently shown to regulate EphA signaling (Egea and Klein, 2007).
evidence: Stated as an unclear aspect in the field, with citation to Egea and Klein, 2007.

claim: EphA activation triggers ADAM10-mediated ephrinA2 cleavage to regulate cell-cell contacts.
source: EphA activation triggers ADAM10-mediated ephrinA2 cleavage to regulate cell-cell contacts (Hattori et al., 2000), whereas binding of ephrinA5 to EphA3 induces an ADAM10-induced trans cleavage of the ligand (Janes et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hattori et al., 2000.

claim: Binding of ephrinA5 to EphA3 induces an ADAM10-induced trans cleavage of the ligand.
source: EphA activation triggers ADAM10-mediated ephrinA2 cleavage to regulate cell-cell contacts (Hattori et al., 2000), whereas binding of ephrinA5 to EphA3 induces an ADAM10-induced trans cleavage of the ligand (Janes et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Janes et al., 2005.

claim: Several Eph receptors and ephrin ligands are cleaved by presenilins (PS: PS1 and PS2), the catalytic component of γ-secretase involved in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease (AD).
source: Notably, several Eph receptors and ephrin ligands are cleaved by presenilins (PS: PS1 and PS2), the catalytic component of γ-secretase involved in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease (AD) (Lleó and Saura, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lleó and Saura, 2011.

claim: EphB2 and ephrinB2 undergo sequential cleavages by metalloproteases and PS/γ-secretase.
source: EphB2 and ephrinB2 undergo sequential cleavages by metalloproteases and PS/γ-secretase, and the ephrinB2 intracellular domain (ICD) resulting from this latter cleavage regulates RhoA through Src kinase in endothelial cells (Georgakopoulos et al., 2006; Litterst et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Georgakopoulos et al., 2006 and Litterst et al., 2007.

claim: The ephrinB2 intracellular domain (ICD) resulting from PS/γ-secretase cleavage regulates RhoA through Src kinase in endothelial cells.
source: EphB2 and ephrinB2 undergo sequential cleavages by metalloproteases and PS/γ-secretase, and the ephrinB2 intracellular domain (ICD) resulting from this latter cleavage regulates RhoA through Src kinase in endothelial cells (Georgakopoulos et al., 2006; Litterst et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Georgakopoulos et al., 2006 and Litterst et al., 2007.

claim: γ-secretase-dependent EphA4 cleavage regulates dendritic spine morphology by affecting Rac signaling.
source: In addition, γ-secretase-dependent EphA4 cleavage regulates dendritic spine morphology by affecting Rac signaling (Inoue et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Inoue et al., 2009.

claim: Cleavage of Eph receptors regulates actin cytoskeleton through alternative mechanisms different from the classical Eph-ephrin signaling.
source: These findings suggest that cleavage of Eph receptors regulates actin cytoskeleton through alternative mechanisms different from the classical Eph-ephrin signaling.
evidence: Inferred from the cited studies on Eph receptor cleavage.

claim: The physiological contribution of Eph receptor shedding on axon growth and whether this event occurs independently of cell-attached ephrins remain unclear.
source: The physiological contribution of Eph receptor shedding on axon growth and whether this event occurs independently of cell-attached ephrins remain still unclear.
evidence: Stated as an unclear aspect in the field.

claim: PS/γ-secretase-dependent EphA3 cleavage mediates axon elongation independently of cell-attached ephrins by promoting filament disassembly and cytoskeleton rearrangement.
source: Here, we found that PS/γ-secretase-dependent EphA3 cleavage mediates axon elongation independently of cell-attached ephrins by promoting filament disassembly and cytoskeleton rearrangement.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental data throughout the study.

claim: Presenilin-1 (PS1; Psen1) is the catalytic component of the γ-secretase complex.
source: Presenilin-1 (PS1; Psen1), the catalytic component of the γ-secretase complex, is mutated in most of familial Alzheimer's disease (AD) cases (De Strooper and Annaert, 2010).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation to De Strooper and Annaert, 2010.

claim: PS1 is mutated in most of familial Alzheimer's disease (AD) cases.
source: Presenilin-1 (PS1; Psen1), the catalytic component of the γ-secretase complex, is mutated in most of familial Alzheimer's disease (AD) cases (De Strooper and Annaert, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to De Strooper and Annaert, 2010.

claim: PS1 is essential for brain development.
source: PS1 is essential for brain development as revealed by abundant brain hemorrhages, enlarged ventricles and neuron migration defects in Psen1-/- mouse embryos (Shen et al., 1997; Hartmann et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shen et al., 1997 and Hartmann et al., 1999.

claim: PS1 binds to and colocalizes with EphA3 in axons and growth cones of hippocampal neurons.
source: PS1 binds to and colocalizes with EphA3 in axons and growth cones of hippocampal neurons, which may explain the axonal, neuronal migration and cortical lamination defects observed in Psen1-/- embryos [(Handler et al., 2000); this study].
evidence: Supported by experimental data in this study and citation to Handler et al., 2000.

claim: Psen1-/- mice die after birth likely due to respiratory failures caused by incomplete lung expansion.
source: Indeed, Psen1-/- mice die after birth likely due to respiratory failures caused by incomplete lung expansion, which resembles the phenotype of Epha3 null mice (Shen et al., 1997; Vaidya et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shen et al., 1997 and Vaidya et al., 2003.

claim: The phenotype of Psen1-/- mice resembles the phenotype of Epha3 null mice.
source: Indeed, Psen1-/- mice die after birth likely due to respiratory failures caused by incomplete lung expansion, which resembles the phenotype of Epha3 null mice (Shen et al., 1997; Vaidya et al., 2003).
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of phenotypes, supported by citations.

claim: Embryonic Epha3 inactivation results in axon misrouting of callosal neurons.
source: Embryonic Epha3 inactivation results in axon misrouting of callosal neurons, although no motor axon targeting abnormalities are observed in Epha3-/- mice (Vaidya et al., 2003; Nishikimi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vaidya et al., 2003 and Nishikimi et al., 2011.

claim: No motor axon targeting abnormalities are observed in Epha3-/- mice.
source: Embryonic Epha3 inactivation results in axon misrouting of callosal neurons, although no motor axon targeting abnormalities are observed in Epha3-/- mice (Vaidya et al., 2003; Nishikimi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vaidya et al., 2003 and Nishikimi et al., 2011.

claim: Epha3/Epha4 deletion causes disturbances in motor axon guidance and sensory-motor neuron assemblies.
source: By contrast, Epha3/Epha4 deletion causes disturbances in motor axon guidance and sensory-motor neuron assemblies (Gallarda et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gallarda et al., 2008.

claim: PS1 regulates axon guidance and kinesin-mediated axonal transport of motor neurons.
source: Similarly, it is well established that PS1 regulates axon guidance and kinesin-mediated axonal transport of motor neurons (Kamal et al., 2001; Bai et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kamal et al., 2001 and Bai et al., 2011.

claim: Loss of function mutations in the presenilin genes sel-12 and hop-1 result in abnormal axonal projections in C. elegans.
source: Loss of function mutations in the presenilin genes sel-12 and hop-1 result in abnormal axonal projections in C. elegans, an effect attributed to altered Notch signaling (Wittenburg et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wittenburg et al., 2000.

claim: Loss of PS1 function results in neurite outgrowth by increasing APP intracellular fragments and activating CREB signaling.
source: While our study indicates that PS1 promotes axonal growth, a recent study demonstrates that loss of PS1 function results in neurite outgrowth by increasing APP intracellular fragments and activating CREB signaling (Deyts et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Deyts et al., 2016.

claim: Inactivation of β-secretase (BACE1) causes axon guidance defects mediated by altered processing of the neural cell adhesion molecule close homolog of L1 (CHL1).
source: Interestingly, inactivation of β-secretase (BACE1), which is involved in APP processing, also causes axon guidance defects mediated by altered processing of the neural cell adhesion molecule close homolog of L1 (CHL1) (Hitt et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hitt et al., 2012.

claim: Proteolytic processing of neuregulin-1 by BACE and ADAM17 proteases mediates myelination of axons in the peripheral nervous system.
source: Moreover, proteolytic processing of neuregulin-1 by BACE and ADAM17 proteases mediates myelination of axons in the peripheral nervous system (Hu et al., 2006; Willem et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hu et al., 2006 and Willem et al., 2006.

claim: Familial-AD linked PS1 mutations cause aberrant APP-dependent axodendritic growth in cultured neurons.
source: Of interest, familial-AD linked PS1 mutations, acting through a partial loss of function mechanism (De Strooper, 2007; Shen and Kelleher, 2007), cause aberrant APP-dependent axodendritic growth in cultured neurons (Pigino et al., 2001; Deyts et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to De Strooper, 2007, Shen and Kelleher, 2007, Pigino et al., 2001, and Deyts et al., 2016.

claim: The PS1/γ-secretase-dependent mechanisms mediating cytoskeleton rearrangement during axon growth have been elusive.
source: Despite these evidences, the PS1/γ-secretase-dependent mechanisms mediating cytoskeleton rearrangement during axon growth have been elusive.
evidence: Stated as an elusive aspect in the field.

claim: PS1/γ-secretase-regulated EphA3 processing is essential for constitutive axon elongation.
source: PS1/γ-secretase-regulated EphA3 processing is essential for constitutive axon elongation as suggested by the mimicking and occluding effects of Epha3 inactivation on axon elongation in PS-deficient neurons.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that Epha3 inactivation mimics and occludes PS deficiency effects.

claim: PS1/γ-secretase-dependent EphA3 cleavage mediates axon elongation independently of classical EphA3 signaling.
source: PS1/γ-secretase-dependent axon growth is independent of classical EphA3 signaling.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that ephrin-A5 does not affect EphA3 processing.

claim: Both ligand-induced EphA3 signaling and blocking ligand-independent EphA3 cleavage inhibit axon growth.
source: In agreement, both ligand-induced signaling and blocking ligand-independent EphA3 cleavage (e.g Epha3 silencing) inhibit axon growth suggesting that both mechanisms occur in cellular conditions.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing effects of both ephrin-A5 and Epha3 silencing.

claim: Both ligand-dependent and ligand-independent EphA3 mechanisms occur in cellular conditions.
source: In agreement, both ligand-induced signaling and blocking ligand-independent EphA3 cleavage (e.g Epha3 silencing) inhibit axon growth suggesting that both mechanisms occur in cellular conditions.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data.

claim: The EphA3 structural conformation is important for mediating axon growth.
source: It is puzzling that not only deletion of the EphA3 C-terminal but also removal of the PDZ or LBD impair recovery of axon length in EphA3- and/or PS1/γ-secretase-deficient neurons, suggesting that the EphA3 structural conformation is important for mediating axon growth.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that multiple EphA3 domain deletions impair axon recovery.

claim: Ligand and neuronal activity regulate PS1/γ-secretase-dependent processing of EphB2 and EphA4.
source: In contrast, both ligand and neuronal activity regulate PS1/γ-secretase-dependent processing of EphB2 and EphA4 (Litterst et al., 2007; Inoue et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Litterst et al., 2007 and Inoue et al., 2009.

claim: Metalloprotease-mediated ephrinA shedding or other intracellular EphA3 effectors may mediate PS-dependent axon elongation.
source: We cannot rule out the possibility that metalloprotease-mediated ephrinA shedding or other intracellular EphA3 effectors mediate PS-dependent axon elongation (Hattori et al., 2000; Janes et al., 2009; Mohamed et al., 2012).
evidence: Speculative statement acknowledging alternative possibilities, with citations.

claim: EphA3 ICD could mediate axon growth by acting through transcriptional mechanisms as described for APP and Notch ICDs.
source: It is also plausible that EphA3 ICD could mediate axon growth by acting through transcriptional mechanisms as described for APP and Notch ICDs (Lleó and Saura, 2011).
evidence: Speculative statement with citation to Lleó and Saura, 2011.

claim: The PS/γ-secretase/EphA3-dependent mechanism mediating axon elongation involves RhoA signaling.
source: The PS/γ-secretase/EphA3-dependent mechanism mediating axon elongation involves RhoA signaling, a pathway implicated in growth cone collapse (Noren and Pasquale, 2004; Hall and Lalli, 2010).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to Noren and Pasquale, 2004 and Hall and Lalli, 2010.

claim: PS1/γ-secretase-deficient neurons show increased RhoA activity.
source: PS1/γ-secretase-deficient neurons show increased RhoA activity, whereas EphA3 ICD inhibits RhoA and reverses axon growth defects.
evidence: Supported by RhoA activity assay data (Figure 5F).

claim: EphA3 ICD inhibits RhoA and reverses axon growth defects.
source: PS1/γ-secretase-deficient neurons show increased RhoA activity, whereas EphA3 ICD inhibits RhoA and reverses axon growth defects.
evidence: Supported by RhoA activity assay and axon length data (Figures 3, 5).

claim: A constitutive active RhoA mutant prevents EphA3 ICD-induced recovery of axon growth.
source: By contrast, a constitutive active RhoA mutant causes the opposite effect, that is, prevents EphA3 ICD-induced recovery of axon growth.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: NMIIA/myosin-9 promotes neurite retraction.
source: Importantly, proteomic analyses revealed that EphA3 ICD interacts with NMIIA heavy chain, a cytoskeleton protein that promotes neurite retraction (Wylie and Chantler, 2003; Gallo, 2006; Kubo et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wylie and Chantler, 2003, Gallo, 2006, and Kubo et al., 2008.

claim: PS1/γ-secretase promotes disassembly or inhibits formation of stable filaments leading to F-actin-mediated axon extension.
source: Nonetheless, our results suggest that PS1/γ-secretase promotes disassembly or inhibits formation of stable filaments leading to F-actin-mediated axon extension.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing changes in NMIIA phosphorylation and localization.

claim: Myosin inhibition induces extension of growth cones and filopodia by reducing retrograde F-actin flow.
source: This idea is consistent with previous findings indicating that myosin inhibition induces extension of growth cones and filopodia by reducing retrograde F-actin flow (Lin et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lin et al., 1996.

claim: EphA3 ICD elevates phosphorylated NMIIA heavy chain and enhances NMIIA/actin colocalization in PS-deficient axons.
source: On the contrary, EphA3 ICD elevates phosphorylated NMIIA heavy chain and enhances NMIIA/actin colocalization in PS-deficient axons, indicating that it induces axon growth by promoting filament disassembly.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claim: EphA3 ICD induces axon growth by promoting filament disassembly.
source: On the contrary, EphA3 ICD elevates phosphorylated NMIIA heavy chain and enhances NMIIA/actin colocalization in PS-deficient axons, indicating that it induces axon growth by promoting filament disassembly.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that EphA3 ICD increases NMIIA phosphorylation, which promotes filament disassembly.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of NMIIA filament assembly reverses axon growth defects in PS/γ-secretase-deficient neurons.
source: Since pharmacological inhibition of NMIIA filament assembly reverses axon growth defects in PS/γ-secretase-deficient neurons, and it does not cause additional effects in the presence of EphA3 ICD, we conclude that PS1/γ-secretase/EphA3 signaling mediates axon growth by promoting disassembly or preventing assembly of axonal NMIIA/actin filaments (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Blebbistatin does not cause additional effects in the presence of EphA3 ICD.
source: Since pharmacological inhibition of NMIIA filament assembly reverses axon growth defects in PS/γ-secretase-deficient neurons, and it does not cause additional effects in the presence of EphA3 ICD, we conclude that PS1/γ-secretase/EphA3 signaling mediates axon growth by promoting disassembly or preventing assembly of axonal NMIIA/actin filaments (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: PS1/γ-secretase/EphA3 signaling mediates axon growth by promoting disassembly or preventing assembly of axonal NMIIA/actin filaments.
source: Since pharmacological inhibition of NMIIA filament assembly reverses axon growth defects in PS/γ-secretase-deficient neurons, and it does not cause additional effects in the presence of EphA3 ICD, we conclude that PS1/γ-secretase/EphA3 signaling mediates axon growth by promoting disassembly or preventing assembly of axonal NMIIA/actin filaments (Figure 7).
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental data showing the effects of PS/γ-secretase, EphA3 ICD, and NMIIA inhibition on axon growth.

claim: The knowledge of NMIIA function in the nervous system is still very limited.
source: The knowledge of NMIIA function in the nervous system is still very limited.
evidence: Stated as a limitation in current knowledge.

claim: EphA3/ephrin-A5 regulates synaptogenesis and septohippocampal projections in the limbic system.
source: Since EphA3/ephrin-A5 regulates synaptogenesis and septohippocampal projections in the limbic system (Yue et al., 2002; Otal et al., 2006), a brain circuit essential for learning, memory and emotional responses, our findings may be relevant for synaptic dysfunction in AD.
evidence: Supported by citations to Yue et al., 2002 and Otal et al., 2006.

claim: The limbic system is a brain circuit essential for learning, memory and emotional responses.
source: Since EphA3/ephrin-A5 regulates synaptogenesis and septohippocampal projections in the limbic system (Yue et al., 2002; Otal et al., 2006), a brain circuit essential for learning, memory and emotional responses, our findings may be relevant for synaptic dysfunction in AD.
evidence: Established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: Septohippocampal projections are severely damaged at early AD stages.
source: Nonetheless, septohippocampal projections are severely damaged at early AD stages (Riekkinen et al., 1987), whereas altered γ-secretase-dependent EphA4 processing was recently associated with synapse pathology in AD brains (Matsui et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Riekkinen et al., 1987.

claim: Altered γ-secretase-dependent EphA4 processing is associated with synapse pathology in AD brains.
source: Nonetheless, septohippocampal projections are severely damaged at early AD stages (Riekkinen et al., 1987), whereas altered γ-secretase-dependent EphA4 processing was recently associated with synapse pathology in AD brains (Matsui et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Matsui et al., 2012.

claim: Myosin NMIIB regulates synaptic actin dynamics during synaptic plasticity and memory.
source: Since myosin NMIIB regulates synaptic actin dynamics during synaptic plasticity and memory (Rex et al., 2010), it will be interesting to study whether NMIIA regulates the function of PS1/γ-secretase on synapses.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rex et al., 2010.

claim: Experimental therapies targeting Eph and myosin are being developed for nerve regeneration and cancer pathologies.
source: Considering the experimental therapies targeting Eph and myosin in nerve regeneration and cancer pathologies (Boyd et al., 2014), it is conceivable that a better understanding of the PS/γ-secretase/EphA3/NMIIA crosstalk may provide new perspectives on common mechanisms regulating human brain development and diseases.
evidence: Supported by citation to Boyd et al., 2014.

claim: A better understanding of the PS/γ-secretase/EphA3/NMIIA crosstalk may provide new perspectives on common mechanisms regulating human brain development and diseases.
source: Considering the experimental therapies targeting Eph and myosin in nerve regeneration and cancer pathologies (Boyd et al., 2014), it is conceivable that a better understanding of the PS/γ-secretase/EphA3/NMIIA crosstalk may provide new perspectives on common mechanisms regulating human brain development and diseases.
evidence: Speculative statement about future implications of the research.
